body:
CONFIRMED 2026-08-24 on the operator's Clara BW, with a positive control later
in time on the same device. An earlier version of this was filed as an open
observation on a six-minute window; the long window settles it.

## The measurement

A disposable highlight was authored on a zero-annotation book, synced, then
removed through the device's own Annotations panel.

    creation   device -> server in about 1 second, correctly typed
    deletion   device tombstone written at 2026-08-23T05:36:06Z
               ... and never uploaded

More than a day later:

    device  Bookmark 665557e8   Hidden='true'   SyncTime = NULL
    server  annotation 665557e8  hidden=0  content_revision=1
            server_modified_at unchanged from creation

## Why this is not deferral

The device kept syncing the whole time, and kept syncing annotations
successfully:

    max Bookmark.SyncTime on the device   2026-08-23T21:24:43Z
    31 of 32 Bookmark rows have SyncTime set; the tombstone is the only NULL

And the control is stronger than "it synced": a dogear the operator created at
2026-08-23T21:23:33 -- roughly sixteen hours AFTER the deletion -- reached the
server at 21:24:43 and is present with `hidden=0`. So the device-to-server
annotation path was demonstrably working, on the same device, after the
deletion was already pending. Creates propagate. Deletions do not.

Note also that Nickel CLEARS `SyncTime` when it writes the tombstone, i.e. it
marks the row as needing upload. It intends to send it and does not.

## Why it matters, and it gets worse rather than better

1. **Today:** a highlight the reader deleted on the device stays live on the
   server and keeps showing in CWNG's web reader. There is no way for them to
   get rid of it from the device.
2. **Soon:** section 11.2 of the two-way design is now closed -- Nickel accepts
   and echoes a CWNG-authored ETag, so server-to-device writeback is viable in a
   way it was not before. Shipping writeback against a server set that still
   contains deletions the user made on-device would **push those highlights back
   onto the device**. The user deletes a highlight, and it comes back.

That is exactly the risk the comment at `cps/readingservices.py` flags next to
`dispatch_annotation_deletes` -- "Nickel can only name annotations Kobo created
... if F-3b565b implements writeback, this provenance authority must be
revisited". This finding is the concrete case that makes it real.

## Root cause: NOT yet established, deliberately

Two candidates remain and they need different fixes:
- Nickel never puts the tombstone in a `deletedAnnotationIds` payload at all
  (device-side; we would have to compensate rather than fix); or
- it does send it and something on our side drops it before
  `dispatch_annotation_deletes` (ours to fix).

The server-side handler itself looks correct on inspection -- it reads
`deletedAnnotationIds` and passes `deletable_sources={"kobo"}`, and the stuck
annotation's source IS `kobo`, so it would be honoured if it arrived.

**Do not guess a fix.** The discriminator is one line of evidence: whether an
`ANNOTATION method=PATCH ... deleted_count=N` handler log appears for a fresh
deletion. The exchange capture landing in this PR records the full PATCH body
and is the instrument for it. Procedure: author a highlight on a zero-annotation
book, sync, delete it via the Annotations panel, then sync with capture enabled
and read whether `deletedAnnotationIds` is present on the wire.

## Residue

The test annotation `665557e8-...` on book 540 is still live on the server,
precisely because the deletion did not propagate. It is one highlight of the
word "son" and it is mine, not the operator's. Left in place so the propagation
question stays re-checkable; clear it with `hidden=1` once the root cause is
settled.
title: A highlight deleted on the Kobo never reaches the server, so it stays live in the web reader and would be resurrected by writeback
